en.title: Education Economics: the whole course
en.short: What education economics covers, how the degree is organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Education economics studies how economic ideas help us understand education, and how education affects the economy. It asks how families, schools, governments and employers decide what education to provide, who pays, who benefits and how resources are used. It also studies returns to schooling, teacher supply, labour markets and inequality.

The course has two sides. One side is economics: scarcity, choice, markets, costs, statistics and policy. The other is teacher education: how people learn, how a syllabus is built, how to teach Economics, how to assess it and how to behave professionally. The two sides meet when you use economics to explain education, and use teaching skills to explain economics.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text: Degrees differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, a B.Ed or B.Sc.(Ed) is commonly a four-year university programme, guided by the National Universities Commission, with teaching practice and education courses alongside Economics. Colleges of education follow the National Commission for Colleges of Education and award the Nigeria Certificate in Education (NCE), not a degree. Ghana and South Africa commonly offer a four-year B.Ed, but titles, entry routes and lengths vary. Some people qualify as teachers through a Postgraduate Diploma in Education (PGDE) after a first degree instead. Always check your own faculty handbook for credit loads, practice periods and award rules.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introduction stage builds foundations. You study the nature and scope of Economics, mathematics and statistics for Economics, and introductory microeconomics and macroeconomics. At the same time you study educational psychology, curriculum foundations and the Economics syllabus, methods of teaching Economics I, and an introduction to the economics of education.

The core stage deepens both sides. In Economics you take intermediate microeconomics and macroeconomics, quantitative methods and introductory econometrics. In education economics you study human capital theory, education production, efficiency and equity, costs and financing, planning and policy, development economics and education, labour markets and education, budgeting and resource management, and comparative and international education economics. In teacher education you study the Economics curriculum and instructional materials, methods of teaching Economics II, assessment and evaluation, teaching practice and microteaching, research methods, and professional ethics.

If you continue to a master’s, the work is more research-based. It includes advanced economics of education, econometric evaluation of education policies, advanced education finance and governance, and a research seminar and dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study Economics as a way of thinking, not a list of facts. For each model, learn the assumptions, draw the graph, work a simple calculation and ask what happens when a condition changes. Keep a glossary of terms and a page of formulas.

For the teaching side, turn theory into practice. Write a short lesson plan for a topic such as demand, teach it to classmates, and note what confused them. Learn to read a syllabus and to match assessment to objectives.

Use past questions and official handbooks. Figures such as fees, salaries, enrolment rates and pass marks change by country and year, so check current official sources. Do not memorise a number without its date and source.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often treat economics as definitions only. They memorise demand and supply without being able to explain a shift, or use a statistic without saying where it came from. Another fault is mixing positive statements, which can be tested, with normative statements, which express a value judgement.

On the teaching side, many students write lesson plans with no clear objective or no assessment. Some talk for the whole lesson and give pupils no task. Others copy a foreign syllabus without checking their own country’s curriculum.

In education economics, a common error is assuming that more spending always raises learning. It may not, if resources are badly used. Another is claiming that education causes higher earnings without considering ability, family background and selection.

keyPoints: Education economics uses economic analysis to study how education is provided, financed and valued.
A teacher-education degree combines Economics with educational psychology, curriculum, methods, assessment and teaching practice.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Study models by their assumptions, graphs and limits, not by memorised definitions alone.
In teaching, clear objectives, pupil activity and matching assessment matter more than long talk.
Statistics and policy claims need a date, a source and care about cause and effect.

en.title: Nature and Scope of Economics
en.short: Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost, micro and macro, positive and normative claims, methods, and links to teaching.

sections.heading: Scarcity and choice
sections.text: Economics studies how people, firms and governments use scarce resources to satisfy wants. Scarcity means resources such as time, land, labour and money are limited while wants are many. It forces choice: choosing one use gives up another. The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative forgone. At a school in Kano, one classroom is free at 9 a.m. and both economics and mathematics classes need it. If economics uses it, the opportunity cost is the mathematics lesson. Opportunity cost is only the best alternative given up.

sections.heading: Micro and macro
sections.text: Microeconomics studies individual units: a household, firm, market or single price. It asks how a student chooses between study and part-time work, or why bread prices rise in one market. Macroeconomics studies the whole economy: national output, unemployment, inflation and government policy. It asks why prices in general rise or unemployment increases. The two connect: many small decisions make up the economy, and economy-wide conditions shape household choices.

sections.heading: Positive and normative
sections.text: A positive statement says what is or will happen and can be tested. “A fee rise reduced enrolment here” is positive. A normative statement says what ought to be and involves values. “Fees should be abolished” is normative. Economics is a social science: it studies human behaviour in society, uses observation and data, and builds models. Unlike physics, it rarely runs controlled experiments, so economists compare cases, use natural experiments and state assumptions. They reason deductively, from general principles to cases, and inductively, from evidence to patterns. Ceteris paribus means other things being equal.

sections.heading: Branches and teaching
sections.text: Main branches include microeconomics, macroeconomics, development economics, labour economics, public economics and international economics. Methods include models, graphs, statistics and clear definitions. For an economics teacher, scope matters: pupils meet scarcity in school budgets and their own time, and must separate positive claims from normative ones. A teacher who uses the classroom example helps students apply economics, not just recite it.

keyPoints: Economics studies how scarce resources are allocated among competing wants.
Scarcity forces choice, and opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone.
Microeconomics studies individual units; macroeconomics studies the whole economy.
Positive statements can be tested; normative statements involve values.
Economics is a social science because it studies human behaviour using evidence and models.
Main branches include micro, macro, development, labour, public and international economics; methods include models, data and ceteris paribus.

en.title: Mathematics for Economics
en.short: Algebra, functions, graphs, equations, percentages, ratios, growth rates and simple optimisation for economics.

sections.heading: Expressions and functions
sections.text:
An algebraic expression combines numbers and variables, such as total cost TC = 50 + 4Q, where Q is output. A function links an input to one output. A linear function has the form y = a + bx; b is the slope, the change in y when x rises by one.

A quadratic function has the form y = ax² + bx + c and its graph is a parabola. In economics, revenue R = 20Q − Q² is quadratic: revenue rises, then falls as price cuts reduce income.

sections.heading: Graphs and equations
sections.text:
Plot points with Q on the horizontal axis and money on the vertical axis. The slope of a straight line is (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁). Simultaneous equations are two equations solved together.

If demand is P = 100 − 2Q and supply is P = 20 + 2Q, set them equal: 100 − 2Q = 20 + 2Q, so 80 = 4Q and Q = 20. Then P = 100 − 40 = 60. Check in supply: 20 + 40 = 60.

sections.heading: Percentages and ratios
sections.text:
Percentage change = (new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100. If school fees rise from 25,000 to 30,000, the change is 5,000 ÷ 25,000 × 100 = 20%.

A ratio compares parts; to share 120 books in the ratio 3:5, total parts = 8, one part = 15, so shares are 45 and 75. Always state units and check that shares add to the total.

sections.heading: Growth and optimisation
sections.text:
Growth rate = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Compound growth uses new = old × (1 + r)^n, where r is a decimal rate and n periods.

Simple optimisation finds a maximum or minimum. For profit π = 40Q − Q² − 100, the maximum is at Q = −b ÷ (2a) = −40 ÷ (2 × −1) = 20. Profit is 40(20) − 20² − 100 = 800 − 400 − 100 = 300. Check arithmetic.

keyPoints: A linear function y = a + bx has slope b; a quadratic y = ax² + bx + c graphs as a parabola.
Solve simultaneous equations by substitution or by setting equal expressions, then check the answer in both equations.
Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100; ratios share a total by dividing it into parts.
Compound growth is new = old × (1 + r)^n, with r written as a decimal.
For y = ax² + bx + c, the turning point is at x = −b ÷ (2a), which gives simple maximum or minimum problems.
Keep units consistent and check every calculation, because a misplaced decimal can change an economic conclusion.

en.title: Statistics and Data for Economics
en.short: This summary covers types of data, sources, sampling, tables, graphs, averages, spread and index numbers for economics.

sections.heading: Data and sampling
sections.text: Economic data are facts about prices, output, employment or education. They may be quantitative (numbers) or qualitative (categories). Quantitative data can be discrete (counts) or continuous (measures). A cross-section compares units at one time; a time series follows one unit over time; a panel follows the same units over time. Primary data are collected by the researcher; secondary data already exist, such as official statistics. Record the source, date, definition and unit. A population is the whole group; a sample is part of it. Random sampling gives every member a known chance of selection. Stratified sampling samples within groups; cluster sampling selects whole groups. Convenience sampling can be biased.

sections.heading: Tables, graphs and averages
sections.text: In a frequency table, list values or class intervals, tally them, and give frequency and relative frequency. Relative frequency = frequency ÷ total. Check that frequencies add to the total. Bar charts compare categories; histograms show continuous intervals; line graphs show time; pie charts show parts. Label axes; start bar charts at zero. Do not cut axes to exaggerate change. The mean is Σx ÷ n. The median is the middle value. The mode is the most frequent value. Range = largest − smallest. Variance is the average of the squared deviations from the mean, and the standard deviation is its square root. For 2, 4, 4, 6, 9: mean = 5; median = 4; mode = 4; range = 7; variance = 5.6; SD ≈ 2.37.

sections.heading: Index numbers and errors
sections.text: An index number compares a value with a base value. A simple price index = (current price ÷ base price) × 100. If a textbook cost 200 naira in the base year and 250 naira now, the index is (250 ÷ 200) × 100 = 125, a rise of 25 per cent. A Laspeyres index uses base-year quantities; a Paasche index uses current-year quantities. Common errors include wrong base years, changing definitions, missing data, sampling bias and misleading graph scales. Ask students to check the source and explain what a number does not show.

keyPoints: Quantitative data are numerical and qualitative data are categorical; data may also be primary or secondary, cross-section, time series or panel.
Record the source, date, definition and unit of every data set, and check that frequencies add to the total.
Random sampling gives every member a known chance; convenience sampling can be biased.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; median is the middle ordered value; mode is the most frequent value; range = largest − smallest; standard deviation = √variance.
Simple price index = (current price ÷ base price) × 100, and the base year and basket must be stated.
Misleading axes, wrong base years, changing definitions, missing data and sampling bias are common sources of error.

en.title: Microeconomics: Foundations
en.short: Scarcity, demand and supply, elasticity, consumer choice, costs, market structures and market failure.

sections.heading: Scarcity and choice
sections.text: Economics studies how people allocate scarce resources. Scarcity means wants exceed the resources available. Every choice has an opportunity cost, the value of the next best option given up. A student who spends an evening studying gives up paid work or rest. Marginal analysis compares the extra benefit of one more unit with its extra cost.

sections.heading: Demand, supply, elasticity
sections.text: Demand is the quantity buyers will take at each price; supply is the quantity sellers will offer. A market clears at equilibrium, where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. A price above equilibrium leaves a surplus and tends to fall; a price below leaves a shortage and tends to rise. Consumer behaviour links preferences and budget limits to demand; utility is satisfaction. Price elasticity of demand measures responsiveness: %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP. Using initial values, if price rises from 100 to 110 and quantity falls from 50 to 45, elasticity is (-5 ÷ 50) ÷ (10 ÷ 100) = -0.10 ÷ 0.10 = -1; the size, 1, means unit elastic. Necessities are usually less elastic than luxuries.

sections.heading: Production and markets
sections.text: Production turns inputs into output. In the short run some inputs are fixed. Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost. Marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit. Profit is maximised where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Market structure describes competition. Perfect competition has many sellers and identical goods; monopoly has one seller; monopolistic competition has differentiated goods; oligopoly has few sellers. Structure affects price, output and efficiency.

sections.heading: Market failure
sections.text: Prices coordinate decisions by carrying information and incentives. They can fail. Externalities are costs or benefits falling on others. Public goods are non-excludable and non-rival. Market power, poor information and inequality also cause failure. Governments may respond with taxes, subsidies, regulation or public provision. For teaching, ask pupils to explain a local price change, such as transport fares, using demand, supply and elasticity.

keyPoints: Scarcity forces choice, and every choice has an opportunity cost.
Equilibrium price equates quantity demanded and quantity supplied.
Price elasticity of demand = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP; absolute value above 1 is elastic.
Consumers maximise utility subject to a budget; total cost = fixed cost + variable cost.
Profit is maximised where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
Market structures differ in competition, and market failure arises from externalities, public goods, market power and poor information.

en.title: Macroeconomics: Foundations
en.short: Measuring national income, inflation and unemployment, and using fiscal and monetary policy.

sections.heading: Measuring output
sections.text: Macroeconomics studies output, jobs, prices and money. Gross domestic product (GDP) is the market value of final goods and services produced in a country in a period. GDP = C + I + G + (X − M), where C is consumption, I is investment, G is government spending, X is exports and M is imports. Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP adjusts for inflation: real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ price index × 100. Gross national income (GNI) adds net income from abroad: income residents earn abroad minus income paid to non-residents. Check the national statistics office for revisions.

sections.heading: Demand and supply
sections.text: Aggregate demand (AD) is total planned spending on domestic output: AD = C + I + G + (X − M). Aggregate supply (AS) is total output firms will produce at each price level. Rising AD can raise output and prices in the short run. In the long run, capacity limits output, so demand growth mainly raises prices. Example: if C = 60, I = 15, G = 20, X = 10 and M = 5, then AD = 60 + 15 + 20 + (10 − 5) = 100. If capacity is 95, demand pressures prices.

sections.heading: Prices, jobs, money
sections.text: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. Inflation rate = (P1 − P0) ÷ P0 × 100. If the index rises from 120 to 126, inflation is (126 − 120) ÷ 120 × 100 = 5%. Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100. If 8 people are unemployed in a labour force of 200, the rate is 4%. Banks create deposits by lending; the central bank sets the policy rate. Higher rates usually reduce borrowing and demand.

sections.heading: Policy tools
sections.text: Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxation. Monetary policy uses interest rates, reserve requirements and open market operations. They affect AD, output, employment and inflation, with delays and trade-offs. In teaching, use circular-flow diagrams and current data. Institutions vary by country; check the central bank and finance ministry.

keyPoints: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M) measures final output.
Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ price index × 100 removes price changes.
AD = C + I + G + (X − M); rising AD can raise output and prices.
Inflation rate = (P1 − P0) ÷ P0 × 100; unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100.
Fiscal policy uses spending and taxation; monetary policy uses interest rates and central bank operations.
Macroeconomic effects have delays and trade-offs, and institutions differ by country.

en.title: Educational Psychology for Economics Teachers
en.short: Learning theories, cognitive development, memory, motivation, differences and classroom planning for economics.

sections.heading: Learning and development
sections.text: Learning theories explain how students gain knowledge. Behaviourism focuses on reinforcement, such as praise and feedback. Cognitivism studies attention, encoding (taking in) and retrieval (recalling). Constructivism says learners build new ideas from prior knowledge. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development (ZPD) is the gap between what a student can do alone and with help. Social learning theory adds modelling (learning by watching and copying others) and self-efficacy, a belief in one’s ability to succeed. Piaget described stages of cognitive development; many adolescents reach formal operations, where abstract and hypothetical reasoning becomes possible. Economics needs such reasoning, so teachers should link models and graphs to concrete cases and surface students’ everyday ideas about prices and jobs.

sections.heading: Memory and motivation
sections.text: Working memory, the short-term store for current thinking, is limited, so new material must be chunked (grouped). Long-term memory depends on organised schemas, which are mental frameworks. Retrieval practice, spacing and worked examples strengthen memory. Transfer means using knowledge in a new context; near transfer stays close to the lesson, while far transfer is harder. Motivation can be intrinsic, from interest, or extrinsic, from rewards. Expectancy-value theory says effort depends on expecting success and valuing the task. Self-efficacy grows through mastery experiences (successes), vicarious (observed) examples and encouragement. For adolescents, relevance helps: link economics to local prices, work and public decisions, while keeping the economics accurate.

sections.heading: Planning for learners
sections.text: Students differ in prior knowledge, reading and numeracy, language, confidence and pace. Teachers should not label fixed learning styles. Instead, plan tiered tasks (tasks at different levels), provide worked examples, allow peer discussion, and offer support or extension. State clear objectives, use short explanations, and check understanding with questions. Use multiple representations: words, tables, graphs and stories. Give guided practice before independent work, and give formative feedback that names the next step. Treat errors as information. A case: after explaining a demand curve, the teacher gives a new market and asks students to predict the direction of change, then discuss why. Review earlier ideas regularly.

keyPoints: Behaviourism, cognitivism, constructivism and social learning theory offer different views of how students learn.
Many adolescents can reason abstractly, but economics models still need concrete examples and scaffolds (temporary support).
Working memory is limited, so chunk new material and use retrieval practice and spacing.
Transfer means applying knowledge in new contexts and is harder when contexts are far apart.
Motivation depends on interest, expected success and value, and self-efficacy grows through mastery.
Plan for differences with tiered tasks, multiple representations, guided practice and feedback.

en.title: Curriculum Foundations and the Economics Syllabus
en.short: Curriculum concepts, aims, content selection, sequencing, and reading an economics syllabus into a scheme of work.

sections.heading: Curriculum and syllabus
sections.text: A curriculum is the whole planned programme of learning: what is taught, why, how and how it is assessed. Usage varies, because some writers use curriculum for the official document and syllabus for a subject list. A syllabus is a subject document that usually gives aims, topics, suggested activities and assessment. A scheme of work is the teacher’s or school’s plan that breaks the syllabus into weeks or lessons. Aims are broad intentions; objectives are specific and measurable, often written with verbs such as explain, calculate or compare.

sections.heading: Choosing and ordering content
sections.text: Content selection asks whether material is accurate, relevant, balanced, feasible and useful for later study. Sequencing arranges it in a teachable order: simple before complex, concrete before abstract, known before unknown, and sometimes chronological. A spiral sequence revisits a topic at a deeper level. For example, Amina, a first-year teacher, receives a syllabus topic called the basic economic problem. She writes an objective: by the end of the lesson, students should explain scarcity, choice and opportunity cost using a local market example. She teaches scarcity before demand and supply, because choice under scarcity underlies both.

sections.heading: Reading a syllabus
sections.text: A school economics syllabus often has a title and level, rationale or aims, learning objectives, content topics, suggested activities and resources, assessment guidance and time allocation. Read it whole before planning. Note the verbs in objectives, the depth expected, prerequisites and assessment. Then build a scheme of work with columns for week, topic, objectives, activities, resources, assessment and remarks. Check that each lesson serves a syllabus objective and that assessment matches it. Syllabuses differ by country, school level, examination body and year. Do not treat one country’s syllabus as universal; use the current official document for your own system.

keyPoints: Curriculum is the whole planned learning programme; a syllabus is the subject document, and a scheme of work breaks it into lessons.
Aims are broad; objectives are specific, measurable and usually begin with an action verb.
Select content for accuracy, relevance, balance, feasibility and usefulness.
Sequence content from simple to complex, concrete to abstract and known to unknown, and revisit key ideas in a spiral.
A syllabus usually contains rationale, objectives, content, activities, resources, assessment and time guidance.
Read the current official syllabus for your country and level, then align each scheme-of-work week to its objectives and assessment.

en.title: Methods of Teaching Economics I
en.short: Lesson planning, exposition, questioning, discussion, examples and basic resources for teaching economics.

sections.heading: Planning a lesson
sections.text:
A lesson plan is a written guide to what learners should achieve, how the teacher will help them, and how learning will be checked. A useful plan states clear objectives, links them to the syllabus, lists materials, sets stages with times, and includes questions and a short evaluation. Objectives should name observable behaviour, for example “students can explain opportunity cost with one local example”.

Practice: write a 10-minute plan for one economics idea, then swap with a partner and check that each stage has a purpose.

sections.heading: Explaining clearly
sections.text:
Exposition means explaining a concept in ordered steps, using simple language and checking understanding. Start from what students know, define new terms, give one example and one non-example, and pause for questions. Clear exposition suits topics with a sequence, such as the circular flow of income or the stages of production.

Practice: explain “scarcity” in 90 seconds to a partner, then ask the partner to repeat it in their own words. If the partner cannot, revise the explanation.

sections.heading: Questions and discussion
sections.text:
Questioning should be planned. Closed questions check recall; open questions ask for reasoning, comparison or prediction. Wait time, the pause after asking, improves answers. Discussion lets students compare views, but needs a clear question and ground rules. It suits policy or welfare topics where more than one view is reasonable, such as whether a government should subsidise education.

Practice: prepare three questions on one topic, one recall, one reasoning, one evaluation, and try them in a small group.

sections.heading: Examples and resources
sections.text:
Examples connect economics to students’ lives. A concrete case, such as a trader in Kano deciding how much stock to buy, can make an abstract idea visible. Teaching resources include the board, handouts, real objects, newspapers and simple charts. Choose a resource only if it supports the objective.

Practice: bring one newspaper price report or a labelled diagram and write two questions it can answer. Avoid using a resource as decoration.

keyPoints: A lesson plan states objectives, stages, materials, questions and evaluation.
Clear exposition moves in ordered steps and checks understanding.
Planned questions should include recall, reasoning and evaluation.
Discussion needs a clear question and ground rules.
Examples and resources should support the lesson objective, not decorate it.
Practice activities help a first-year teacher test explanation and questioning.

en.title: Introduction to the Economics of Education
en.short: Education as consumption and investment; costs, benefits and financing; and how it differs from economics education.

sections.heading: What the field studies
sections.text: The economics of education applies economic ideas to education. Education is an economic activity: it uses scarce resources, such as teachers’ time, buildings and books, that have other possible uses. Choosing one use means giving up another, and the value of the best alternative given up is the opportunity cost. The field studies the costs, benefits, financing and outcomes of education, using the tools of economics.

sections.heading: Consumption or investment
sections.text:
Education is consumption because people value learning for its own sake and use schooling now. It is also investment: resources are spent today in the hope of returns later. Those returns include higher earnings, better health and wider social benefits. The skills and knowledge a person carries are called human capital.

A simple example shows the idea. Suppose one year of study costs 200,000 in fees and the student gives up 300,000 in wages. The cost is 200,000 + 300,000 = 500,000. If the extra earnings afterwards are 100,000 a year, the cost is recovered in 500,000 ÷ 100,000 = 5 years, before interest.

sections.heading: Questions the field asks
sections.text: The field asks four broad questions. Costs: what does a year of schooling cost, and who bears it? Benefits: what do individuals and society gain, and how large are private and social returns? Financing: should education be paid for by taxes, fees, loans or vouchers, and how should the burden be shared between government, households and employers? Outcomes: does extra spending actually improve learning, and who gets access?

sections.heading: Two similar names
sections.text: Two similar names mean different things. Economics education is the teaching of Economics as a school subject: its syllabus, methods and assessment. The economics of education is the economic study of education as a whole sector. A teacher of Economics needs both, but they are not the same.

keyPoints: The economics of education applies economic analysis to education as a sector; economics education is the teaching of Economics as a school subject.
Education is both consumption, valued now, and investment, costing now and yielding returns later.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up.
Human capital is the skills and knowledge people carry.
Costs include direct costs such as fees and books plus forgone earnings.
The field asks about costs, benefits, financing and outcomes, and about who gains access.

en.title: Intermediate Microeconomics: Models and Their Limits
en.short: Consumer choice, production and cost, market structures, welfare and market failure with diagrams.

sections.heading: Consumer choice
sections.text:
A budget constraint shows affordable bundles: PxX + PyY = M. With Px = 2, Py = 4 and M = 40, the intercepts are 20 units of X or 10 units of Y. An indifference curve joins bundles giving equal utility. At the best affordable bundle the curve touches the budget line, so the marginal rate of substitution MRS = Px/Py = 0.5. A price change rotates the line and splits the response into substitution and income effects. Limitations: real people may not calculate, preferences can change, and indifference curves are hard to observe.

When teaching, draw the budget line first, then add one indifference curve and show the tangency point.

sections.heading: Production and cost
sections.text: A production function maps inputs to output. With Q = 2L and wage w = 10, variable cost is 10L = 5Q. Adding fixed cost 20 gives TC = 20 + 5Q, so marginal cost is 5 and average total cost falls as Q rises. Isoquants show input mixes for one output; cost curves follow from input prices and returns to scale. Limitations: firms may not know their functions, and fixed inputs vary by time horizon.

sections.heading: Market structures
sections.text: Perfect competition has many small firms, identical goods and free entry; price equals marginal cost in long-run equilibrium. A monopoly faces the market demand curve and sets output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, usually with a higher price and lower output. Monopolistic competition has differentiated products; oligopoly has few firms and strategic behaviour. Diagrams show profit, output and deadweight loss. Limitations: real markets are mixed, and models assume known demand and stable costs.

sections.heading: Welfare and failure
sections.text: Welfare economics compares consumer surplus, producer surplus and total surplus. A competitive equilibrium maximises total surplus under strict assumptions; a monopoly or tax creates deadweight loss. Market failure includes externalities, public goods, common resources and asymmetric information. For teaching, ask students to draw the before-and-after diagrams and calculate the loss. Limitations: distributional fairness is not settled by efficiency alone, and real policy needs evidence.

keyPoints: Budget constraint: PxX + PyY = M; the best bundle has MRS = Px/Py.
Production function Q = f(L,K); total cost TC = FC + VC and marginal cost MC = ΔTC/ΔQ.
Perfect competition gives P = MC in the long run; a monopoly sets MR = MC.
Total surplus = consumer surplus + producer surplus; deadweight loss measures lost surplus.
Market failure includes externalities, public goods, common resources and asymmetric information.
Diagrams are models: check assumptions and data before using them for policy.

en.title: Intermediate Macroeconomics: Models and Policy
en.short: AD-AS, multiplier, inflation and unemployment, money, fiscal and monetary policy, open economy basics.

sections.heading: Models and views
sections.text:
Intermediate macroeconomics models the whole economy. Aggregate demand (AD) is total planned spending at each price level. Aggregate supply (AS) is total output firms will produce at each price level. Short-run AS slopes upward because wages and prices are sticky, meaning slow to adjust. Long-run AS is vertical at potential output, set by resources and technology.

Keynesian models stress sticky prices and demand-led unemployment. Monetarist and new classical models stress flexible prices, expectations and market clearing. New Keynesian models keep sticky prices but add expectations and rules. Models guide policy.

sections.heading: Multiplier and cycles
sections.text:
The multiplier shows how initial spending changes equilibrium income. In a simple closed economy, multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC), where MPC is the marginal propensity to consume, the fraction of extra income spent. If MPC = 0.8, multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5. A 20 billion rise in autonomous spending raises income by 20 × 5 = 100 billion, assuming spare capacity and no crowding out. Crowding out is the fall in private spending when public borrowing raises interest rates.

Inflation is a sustained rise in the price level. Unemployment is people willing and able to work but without jobs. The short-run Phillips curve suggests a trade-off; the long-run curve is often vertical at the natural rate.

sections.heading: Money and openness
sections.text:
Money demand is the wish to hold cash and deposits for transactions, precaution and speculation. Money supply is created by banks and influenced by the central bank. Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxation; monetary policy sets interest rates or money growth. IS-LM shows fiscal policy shifting IS and monetary policy shifting LM.

Monetarists favour stable money growth; Keynesians accept active fiscal policy in deep recessions; new classical economists expect anticipated policy to be ineffective if expectations are rational. In an open economy, the balance of payments records trade and finance, and the exchange rate is one currency’s price in another. Floating rates let monetary policy target domestic goals; fixed rates must defend the parity.

keyPoints: AD is total planned spending; short-run AS slopes upward because prices are sticky, while long-run AS is vertical at potential output.
The simple multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − MPC); with MPC = 0.8 it is 5, so a 20 billion rise in autonomous spending raises income by 100 billion when there is spare capacity.
Keynesian, monetarist, new classical and new Keynesian views differ mainly on price flexibility, expectations and the case for active policy.
Inflation is a sustained rise in the price level; the short-run Phillips curve shows a possible trade-off with unemployment, but the long-run curve is often vertical at the natural rate.
Money demand is the wish to hold cash and deposits; money supply is created by banks and influenced by the central bank.
Fiscal policy uses spending and taxation, monetary policy sets interest rates or money growth, and in an open economy the exchange rate regime limits policy.

en.title: Quantitative Methods and Introductory Econometrics
en.short: This summary covers hypothesis tests, correlation, OLS regression, assumptions, data problems and causation.

sections.heading: Testing and correlation
sections.text: Hypothesis testing sets a null hypothesis H0, often no effect, against an alternative H1. Choose a significance level α, commonly 0.05. A test statistic compares an estimate with its hypothesised value, for example t = (estimate − hypothesised value) ÷ standard error. The p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme if H0 is true; reject H0 if p < α. The correlation coefficient r measures the direction and strength of a linear association, from −1 to +1. For study hours and scores (2,50), (4,60), (6,65), (8,75), (10,80), r = 150 ÷ √(40 × 570) ≈ 0.99.

sections.heading: Regression and OLS
sections.text: Simple regression models y = β0 + β1x + u, where y is outcome, x explanatory variable, β0 intercept, β1 slope and u error. Ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses estimates b0 and b1 that minimise the sum of squared residuals. Here b1 = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ Σ(x − x̄)² = 150 ÷ 40 = 3.75, and b0 = ȳ − b1x̄ = 66 − 3.75 × 6 = 43.5. The fitted line is score = 43.5 + 3.75 × hours. Multiple regression adds variables: y = β0 + β1x1 + ... + βkxk + u. A coefficient is the associated change in y for a one-unit rise in that x, holding others constant.

sections.heading: Assumptions and data problems
sections.text: OLS is unbiased if E(u|x) = 0. Other assumptions include linearity in parameters, a random sample, no perfect collinearity, and homoskedasticity for the usual standard errors. Education data often break these conditions. Omitted variables, measurement error, selection and reverse causality cause endogeneity, so estimates may be biased. Multicollinearity makes coefficients imprecise; heteroskedasticity distorts standard errors; missing data can bias results.

sections.heading: Causation and teaching
sections.text: Correlation is not causation: a third factor, reverse causality or selection can explain an association. Random assignment or natural experiments give stronger causal evidence. In teaching, use local school data; ask students to interpret coefficients and question causal claims.

keyPoints: A hypothesis test compares an estimate with a null value using t = (estimate − hypothesised value) ÷ standard error, and rejects H0 when p < α.
The correlation coefficient r lies between −1 and +1 and measures only linear association.
OLS estimates in y = β0 + β1x + u minimise the sum of squared residuals.
In multiple regression y = β0 + β1x1 + ... + βkxk + u, each coefficient is interpreted holding the other variables constant.
OLS is unbiased when E(u|x) = 0; omitted variables, measurement error, selection and reverse causality can violate this.
Correlation does not prove causation; random assignment or natural experiments give stronger causal evidence.

en.title: Human Capital Theory and Returns to Education
en.short: Education as an investment, private and social returns, estimation methods and criticisms.

sections.heading: Education as investment
sections.text:
Human capital is the knowledge, skills and health that raise productivity. Human capital theory treats education as an investment: spend now for future benefits. Private costs are what the student or family pays, including tuition, books, transport and foregone earnings, the income given up while studying. Private benefits include higher pay and better job prospects.

Social costs and benefits are society’s totals, including public spending and external benefits. Some benefits are hard to measure.

sections.heading: Estimating returns
sections.text:
Economists compare costs and benefits over time using present value: PV = Σ (B_t − C_t) ÷ (1 + r)^t, with discount rate r. The internal rate of return is the r that makes PV zero. The Mincer equation, ln Y = a + bS + cX + dX², where S is years of schooling and X experience, gives b as the return to one more year of schooling.

Example: a one-year course costs 100,000 directly and 50,000 in foregone earnings, total 150,000. It raises earnings by 30,000 a year for ten years. Undiscounted benefit is 300,000, net 150,000. At 10%, benefit present value is 30,000 × [1 − (1.10)^−10] ÷ 0.10 = 184,337, so net present value is about 34,337 and the return exceeds 10%.

sections.heading: Why estimates vary
sections.text:
Estimates vary by country because labour markets, wage levels, education quality and costs differ. They vary by level of education, which has different costs and earnings premiums. They vary by year with economic conditions, policy and data.

Methods matter: years of schooling, qualifications, discount rate, ability and family background controls, and private versus social returns.

sections.heading: Criticisms
sections.text:
Criticisms: the screening hypothesis says education may mainly signal existing ability rather than create it. Credentialism and overeducation can lower real returns. Estimates may omit ability, family background and selection.

It may undercount non-market benefits, and measured returns can be distorted by discrimination and unequal access. For teaching, it explains investment in economics education but is not the only view.

keyPoints: Human capital is the knowledge, skills and health that raise productivity, and education is treated as an investment in it.
Private costs include tuition, books, transport and foregone earnings; private benefits include higher earnings and better jobs.
Social returns count public costs and external benefits, and they are harder to measure than private returns.
Present value is PV = Σ (B_t − C_t) ÷ (1 + r)^t, and the internal rate of return is the r that makes PV zero.
The Mincer equation ln Y = a + bS + cX + dX² estimates b as the return to one more year of schooling.
Returns vary by country, level and year, and criticisms include screening, credentialism, omitted ability and ignored non-market benefits.

en.title: Education Production, Efficiency and Equity
en.short: Inputs, value added, technical and allocative efficiency, equity and measurement problems.

sections.heading: Production and value added
sections.text: An education production function models how inputs produce learning. Inputs include teachers and their quality, materials, school time, class size and family support. Outputs include test scores, completion and wider skills. Raw scores reflect home background and prior learning, so researchers use value-added measures. These compare later attainment with earlier attainment or with predicted attainment. If a pupil moves from 50 to 60, the gain is 10 points; another moving from 65 to 70 gains 5. The second has the higher score, but the first has the larger gain. Value added is not a pure school effect: tests are narrow and data may be missing.

sections.heading: Technical and allocative efficiency
sections.text: Technical efficiency means getting the most learning from given inputs, or using the least input to reach a learning target. If School A reaches an average score of 60 with two teachers and 40 teaching hours, while School B reaches 60 with three teachers and 50 hours, A is technically more efficient in that comparison, if pupils and measures are similar. Allocative efficiency asks whether the mix of inputs and outputs serves society’s goals. A school may raise exam scores efficiently but neglect critical thinking or equitable access. Efficiency is not merely cutting cost; it concerns valued outcomes.

sections.heading: Equity and measurement
sections.text: Equity concerns fairness: equal access, fair treatment and support for disadvantaged learners. Horizontal equity treats similar learners similarly; vertical equity gives more support where need is greater. Measurement is difficult. Learning has many dimensions, school resources are hard to count, and families choose schools, so simple comparisons can be biased. Findings on whether more resources raise learning vary by country, schooling phase, outcome and data quality. Some studies find resources matter mainly where they are very scarce or when they change teaching quality; others find teacher quality and classroom practice matter more than buildings. Treat single studies with caution and check current official data.

keyPoints: An education production function, learning = f(inputs), relates teachers, materials and school time to learning outputs.
Value added = later score − earlier score, or actual score − predicted score; it is an imperfect school effect.
Technical efficiency means maximum learning from given inputs, or minimum inputs for a given learning target.
Allocative efficiency asks whether the input and output mix serves society’s valued goals, not just exam scores.
Equity includes equal access, fair treatment and extra support for greater need.
Findings on school resources vary because outcomes, contexts, data and family background differ; check current evidence.

en.title: Costs and Financing of Education
en.short: Private and social costs, cost analysis, and how education is financed through public funds, fees and cost-sharing.

sections.heading: Private and social costs
sections.text: Private costs are what a student or household pays or gives up: fees, books, transport and earnings lost while studying. Social costs are all costs to society, including private costs and public spending on teachers, buildings and equipment. A policy may look cheap to a family but costly to the public budget.

sections.heading: Direct and indirect costs
sections.text: Direct costs are actual payments for inputs: tuition, salaries, textbooks and electricity. Indirect costs, also called opportunity costs, are not paid directly for the service; examples are students’ forgone earnings or a building that could earn rent. Recurrent costs recur each year, such as salaries and supplies. Capital costs are one-off items, such as buildings and vehicles. Countries classify and share these costs differently, so check current national rules and school accounts.

sections.heading: Comparing options
sections.text: Cost-effectiveness analysis compares programmes with the same outcome. Cost per unit of effect = cost ÷ effect. If Programme A costs 100,000 and raises a test score by 10 points, cost per point is 100,000 ÷ 10 = 10,000. If Programme B costs 60,000 and raises it by 5 points, cost per point is 60,000 ÷ 5 = 12,000. A is more cost-effective per point, though B costs less in total. Cost-benefit analysis values benefits in money: net benefit = benefits − costs; benefit-cost ratio = benefits ÷ costs. Future amounts should be discounted to present value, because money received later is worth less than the same amount today. If benefits are 150,000 and costs 100,000, net benefit is 50,000 and the ratio is 1.5. Both methods depend on assumptions, so state them.

sections.heading: Sources of finance
sections.text: Education is financed by public budgets, household fees and donations. Public funding comes from taxes. Fees shift cost to households. Cost-sharing means government, families, communities and employers share costs. Each source has trade-offs: fees raise funds but may exclude poor students; public funding protects access but competes with other public needs. Arrangements differ by country, so check policy.

keyPoints: Private costs fall on students and households, while social costs include all costs to society.
Direct costs are actual payments for inputs, and indirect costs are opportunity costs such as forgone earnings.
Cost-effectiveness analysis compares cost per unit of effect: cost ÷ effect.
Cost-benefit analysis compares money benefits with costs: net benefit = benefits − costs, and benefit-cost ratio = benefits ÷ costs.
Public funding, fees and cost-sharing each involve trade-offs between raising funds, access and fairness.
Financing rules and the balance of public and private funding differ by country, so check current official policy.

en.title: Education Planning and Policy
en.short: Manpower, social demand and cost-benefit planning, the policy cycle, implementation and evaluation.

sections.heading: Planning approaches
sections.text: Education planning sets targets for places, teachers and facilities and decides how to reach them. Manpower planning forecasts the workers the economy will need, by occupation and education level, then adjusts enrolments to avoid shortages or surpluses. It assumes forecasts are reliable and that graduates take the expected jobs. Social demand planning starts from households’ demand for schooling and asks how many places to provide; it is responsive but may ignore labour-market needs. Cost-benefit planning compares the costs of a project with its expected benefits, usually as present values because benefits come later. Illustrative example: costs of 500,000 per student and extra earnings of 800,000 give a simple benefit-cost ratio of 800,000 ÷ 500,000 = 1.6; above 1 suggests benefits exceed costs, but proper appraisal discounts future earnings and counts only the extra effect.

sections.heading: Policy cycle
sections.text: Policy is made in stages: problem identification and agenda setting, formulation of options, adoption by decision-makers, implementation, and evaluation. The cycle is not linear; evaluation can send a policy back to the agenda. Good formulation states objectives, targets, costs, responsibilities and a timeline. It also identifies assumptions, such as teacher supply or budget release, that must hold.

sections.heading: Implementation gap
sections.text: Implementation often differs from design because plans meet real constraints. Funds may arrive late, data may be weak, classrooms may be unavailable, and teachers may refuse rural posts. Politics, administrative capacity and incentives shape what happens. A plan that assumes 500 new teachers but deploys only 300 will miss its enrolment target unless class sizes or training change. Implementation needs clear roles, timely funding, monitoring and local consultation.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: Evaluation judges whether a policy met its objectives and at what cost. It can assess inputs, processes, outputs and outcomes. Good evaluation compares results with a counterfactual, the situation without the policy, and feeds lessons into the next cycle. In teaching, the same logic helps a department plan resources and review its own economics programme.

keyPoints: Manpower planning forecasts labour needs; social demand planning responds to household demand for places.
Cost-benefit planning compares discounted benefits with costs; benefit-cost ratio = present value of benefits ÷ present value of costs, and above 1 suggests benefits exceed costs.
The policy cycle runs from agenda setting through formulation, adoption, implementation and evaluation.
Implementation differs from design because of funding delays, weak data, capacity limits, politics and incentives.
Evaluation compares outcomes with a counterfactual and feeds lessons into the next policy cycle.
Plans need clear targets, costs, responsibilities and timelines.

en.title: Economics Curriculum and Instructional Materials
en.short: This summary covers schemes of work, lesson sequences, resources and materials evaluation for economics teaching.

sections.heading: Planning the term
sections.text:
A scheme of work is a term plan listing, week by week, topics, objectives, activities, materials and assessment. It turns the syllabus into teachable steps. A lesson sequence orders one topic: recall prior knowledge, explain, model an example, guide practice, then check understanding.

In economics, teach definitions before graphs and graphs before policy. For example, demand and supply, then equilibrium, then price controls. In Nigeria, follow the current national curriculum and state guidelines; check the latest official version because they change.

sections.heading: Resources and alignment
sections.text:
Instructional materials are anything that helps learning: textbooks, charts, worksheets, newspaper cuttings, market price data, videos, spreadsheets and simulations. Local materials make economics concrete. A class can record prices in a local market and plot them. Digital resources add simulations and open educational resources, but check offline access, devices, copyright and student data. Manage them by storing safely, sharing within the department and budgeting for replacement.

Alignment means the objective, activity and assessment ask for the same learning. If the objective is “students will calculate price elasticity of demand”, the activity should use price and quantity data, and the assessment should require a calculation, not only a definition. Use measurable verbs such as define, calculate, explain and evaluate.

sections.heading: Evaluating materials
sections.text:
Evaluate a material for accuracy, level and bias. Accuracy: check definitions, figures, graphs, dates and worked answers. Level: check reading difficulty, mathematical demand and assumed background. Bias: check whose examples, names, places and jobs appear, and whether poor, rural, female or minority experience is missing or stereotyped.

Case: Mr Ade, an invented teacher in Ibadan, finds a textbook that defines inflation correctly but uses only European prices. He keeps the definition, adds Nigerian market data and asks students to compare. He notes the source and date. This keeps the material accurate and local without copying errors.

keyPoints: A scheme of work turns the syllabus into a weekly plan of objectives, activities, materials and assessment.
A lesson sequence moves from prior knowledge through explanation and guided practice to independent application and checking.
Instructional materials include textbooks, local data and digital resources; check access, copyright and data protection.
Alignment means objectives, activities and assessment require the same kind of learning.
Evaluate materials for accuracy, level and bias, including whose examples and experiences are represented.
In Nigeria, follow the current national curriculum and state guidelines, and check for updates.

en.title: Advanced Methods of Teaching Economics
en.short: Problem-based learning, cases, simulations, projects, group work, differentiation and ICT in economics.

sections.heading: Choosing methods
sections.text: Advanced methods give students more control. Problem-based learning (PBL) starts with a real problem that students must explain or solve; it suits open-ended topics such as market failure or unemployment. Case studies are short narratives of a real or realistic decision; they suit policy and business economics. Simulations imitate a market or institution, such as a trading game, and help students feel constraints. Project work is an extended inquiry, often over weeks, and suits data collection and report writing. Cooperative learning means structured small-group work with shared goals. Differentiated instruction adapts tasks, support and assessment to different readiness levels. ICT means information and communication technology: phones, computers, projectors and online resources.

sections.heading: Case in practice
sections.text: In a class of 120, Mrs Adeyemi teaches a unit on competition. She writes a one-page case about Mama Ngozi, a fictional trader whose sales fall when a new shop opens. Each group of six reads the case, lists the economic question, names the data needed and proposes one action. Only one copy per group is needed. Groups present for two minutes. A short rubric scores the question, evidence and reasoning. Peer assessment, where students score each other’s work, keeps marking manageable. This is a case study plus cooperative learning; it is not a full PBL cycle because the problem is short and the inquiry ends in one lesson. In PBL the problem drives learning over several sessions.

sections.heading: Large classes and resources
sections.text:
Large classes need routines. Set group roles (reader, recorder, timekeeper, reporter), use a visible timer, and give a one-page task sheet. Use peer assessment and sample answers.

For limited resources, use local examples, paper-based simulations with beans or tokens, shared phones, offline videos and community data. ICT can support quizzes and feedback, but do not depend on electricity or internet. Plan a backup.

keyPoints: Problem-based learning starts with a real problem; case studies use short decision narratives.
Simulations imitate markets or institutions; project work is extended inquiry.
Cooperative learning uses structured groups with shared goals; differentiation adapts tasks to readiness.
ICT includes phones, computers and online resources, but plan for power and connectivity failures.
Large classes need group roles, timers, task sheets and peer assessment.
Use local examples and paper-based materials when resources are limited.

en.title: Assessment and Evaluation in Economics Education
en.short: Formative and summative assessment, test construction, marking, feedback, validity, reliability and fairness.

sections.heading: Formative and summative
sections.text: Assessment gathers evidence of learning; evaluation judges that evidence against goals. Formative assessment happens during teaching to guide the next lesson. Examples are a short quiz, a think-pair-share or an exit ticket. Summative assessment happens at the end, for example a terminal examination, and usually gives a grade. Both need clear learning outcomes, stated as what students can do, such as “explain how a price ceiling creates a shortage”.

sections.heading: Building valid tests
sections.text: A good test is valid, reliable and fair. Validity means it measures the intended outcomes, not just memory. Reliability means it gives consistent results across markers or occasions. Fairness means no group is disadvantaged by language, context or access. Use a table of specifications (test blueprint) to match items to topics and cognitive levels. Write questions that test understanding: ask students to predict, compare, interpret data or apply a model to a new case. Avoid items answerable by recalling a definition. For example, instead of “Define opportunity cost”, ask: “A student can study or work. Explain the opportunity cost of studying and identify one hidden cost.”

sections.heading: Marking and feedback
sections.text: Mark with a scheme written before marking. Mark anonymously where possible, and moderate a sample to keep standards consistent. Give feedback that is specific, timely and actionable: say what was good, what was wrong and what to do next. Correct errors in reasoning, not only final answers.

sections.heading: Using results
sections.text: Use results to improve teaching. Item analysis shows which questions were too easy, too hard or did not discriminate. If 30 of 40 students answered an item correctly, its difficulty index is 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75, or 75 per cent; a high value means the item was easy. If an item is answered correctly by most students in the top group but few in the bottom group, it discriminates well. A case: Mrs Adeyemi finds that many students confuse a shift in demand with a movement along the curve. She reteaches with two diagrams and a new quiz. Record the change.

keyPoints: Formative assessment guides teaching during a course; summative assessment grades learning at the end.
Validity means a test measures the intended outcomes; reliability means consistent results; fairness means no group is disadvantaged.
A table of specifications matches test items to topics and cognitive levels.
Questions that ask students to predict, compare, interpret or apply test understanding better than questions that ask for definitions.
Mark with a prepared scheme, moderate samples, and give specific, timely feedback.
Item difficulty p = number correct ÷ number tested, where a high p means the item was easy; use item analysis and student errors to reteach weak areas.

en.title: Teaching Practice and Microteaching
en.short: Preparing, teaching and evaluating observed economics lessons, with feedback and reflection.

sections.heading: Microteaching first
sections.text: Microteaching is a short, scaled-down lesson taught to a small group, often peers, and usually recorded or observed. It lets you practise one skill, such as explaining demand, asking questions or closing a lesson, before school placement. Prepare a short plan: state what pupils should know or do by the end, list materials, set the steps and timing, and choose how you will check learning. Keep the economics correct: define terms, use a simple example, and avoid unsupported claims.

sections.heading: Planning the lesson
sections.text: Teaching practice, or practicum, is a supervised period in a school. Begin with the scheme of work, the school’s plan of topics by term, and the syllabus. Write a lesson plan with clear objectives, prior knowledge, materials, teacher and learner activities, timing and assessment. Prepare examples from familiar settings. In a case, Ada plans a lesson on scarcity for a secondary class. She uses a market scene in Kano, asks pupils to list scarce resources, and sets a short group task. She checks her definitions against the textbook.

sections.heading: Teaching and managing
sections.text: Arrive early, dress and speak professionally, and follow school rules. Start with a brief review, share the objective, explain in small steps, question all pupils, and use wait time, a short pause after a question. Classroom management means preventing disruption through clear routines, movement, voice and fair rules. If a pupil disrupts, respond calmly and privately where possible. Keep to time and leave a few minutes for summary and assessment.

sections.heading: Feedback and evaluation
sections.text: After the lesson, invite peer and supervisor feedback. Ask for specific evidence: what worked, what confused pupils, and what to change. Separate feedback on economics accuracy from feedback on teaching. Reflective practice means examining what you planned, what happened, why, and what you will do next. Evaluation uses the lesson objective and evidence of learning, not only enjoyment. Your institution’s grading and pass rules vary, so check the current handbook.

keyPoints: Microteaching is a short observed lesson used to practise one teaching skill before school placement.
A practicum lesson is planned from the scheme of work and syllabus with clear objectives, activities, timing and assessment.
Teach in small steps, question all pupils and manage routines calmly and fairly.
Peer and supervisor feedback should be specific and evidence-based.
Reflective practice links what happened to what you will change next.
Check your institution’s current rules for supervision, grading and professional conduct.

en.title: Development Economics and Education
en.short: Covers education in growth, poverty, inequality, human development, returns and access-quality-equity debates.

sections.heading: Growth and human development
sections.text:
Development economics studies long-run improvement in living standards, not only GDP. Education raises worker skills and helps firms adopt technology, so it can support growth. It also matters directly: literacy, numeracy and health knowledge are part of human development, meaning the expansion of people’s choices and capabilities. Growth can occur without broad schooling, and schooling may not raise growth if learning is weak.

For example, if 60 of 100 workers are literate, raising this to 80 adds 20 potentially skilled workers, but only if learning is real.

sections.heading: Poverty and inequality
sections.text:
Education can reduce poverty by raising earnings and improving health and farm decisions. But access is uneven. Poor households face fees, transport costs, child labour and lost work. Girls and rural children often lag. Education can also widen inequality if returns go mainly to advantaged groups.

In an invented rural district, a new school raises enrolment, but dropout stays high among children who walk far or work at the market. Policy must address costs, safety and support, not just buildings.

sections.heading: Returns to education
sections.text:
Returns to education compare extra earnings with costs. Private returns go to the individual; social returns include spillovers but subtract public costs. In developing economies, estimates vary widely, and school quality matters. Mincer estimates, which regress log earnings on schooling and experience, can be biased by ability and quality.

Example: a one-year course costs 500 units, including forgone earnings, and raises annual earnings by 100 units for 10 years. Undiscounted gain = 100 × 10 = 1,000; net gain = 1,000 − 500 = 500. Discounting lowers the gain.

sections.heading: Access, quality, equity
sections.text:
Policy debates balance access, quality and equity. Access asks who can enrol and stay. Quality asks what students learn, measured by literacy and numeracy tests, not only enrolment. Equity asks whether poor, rural, girls and disabled students get fair support.

These goals compete for budget. A government may choose free primary schooling, teacher training or targeted scholarships. Evidence should guide choices, but values matter.

keyPoints: Development is broader than GDP; education supports growth and human development.
Education reduces poverty through earnings, health and choices, but unequal access can widen inequality.
Private returns accrue to the individual; social returns include spillovers and subtract public costs.
Returns estimates vary in developing economies, and school quality, ability bias and credentialism affect them.
Policy debates balance access, quality and equity, and choices involve budget trade-offs.
A simple private return is (extra earnings − costs) ÷ costs × 100%; the Mincer form is ln(earnings) = a + bS + cX + dX².

en.title: Labour Markets and Education
en.short: How education links to earnings, productivity, signalling, mismatch and graduate unemployment.

sections.heading: Education and earnings
sections.text:
A labour market is where workers supply skills and employers demand them. Demand for labour is derived: it depends on demand for the goods and services workers help to produce.

Human capital theory (Schultz, Becker) holds that education builds skills, raises productivity and so raises pay. Studies in many countries find more schooling goes with higher earnings, but the gap varies widely by country, level and field of study, and part of it reflects ability, family background and location.

sections.heading: Signalling and screening
sections.text:
A competing explanation is signalling. In Spence’s model schooling may add little productivity; a certificate signals ability that was already there, because abler people find study easier to finish. Screening (Arrow) says employers use credentials as a cheap filter when ability is hard to see.

Both predict a premium without a matching productivity gain. The sheepskin effect, a jump in pay at the certificate itself rather than smoothly with each year, fits this. Most economists treat the two views as complements.

sections.heading: Mismatch and unemployment
sections.text:
Skills mismatch takes two forms. Vertical mismatch is holding more or less education than the job needs; horizontal mismatch is a field of study unrelated to the job. Both can lower pay and job satisfaction.

Education does not guarantee work: graduate unemployment can coexist with unfilled vacancies through mismatch or costly job search, and weak demand for graduates is a further cause. Labour markets differ by country. In Nigeria and much of Africa informal work, self-employment and public employment are large; Germany’s apprenticeship system ties school to firms. Findings do not transfer automatically.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Invented figures. A graduate earns 180,000 naira a month, a secondary-school leaver 120,000. The premium is (180,000 − 120,000) ÷ 120,000 = 60,000 ÷ 120,000 = 0.50, or 50 per cent.

Costs come early, gains later, so future earnings are discounted: 60,000 received a year from now at 10 per cent is worth 60,000 ÷ 1.10 = 54,545 today. For class, use current national data, not textbook figures.

keyPoints: Labour demand is derived from demand for the goods and services workers produce.
Human capital theory says schooling raises productivity and pay; signalling and screening say credentials mainly reveal existing ability.
Earnings premium = (higher earnings − lower earnings) ÷ lower earnings.
Present value = amount ÷ (1 + r)^t, because gains arrive after costs.
Vertical mismatch is over- or under-education for a job; horizontal mismatch is a field of study unrelated to the job.
Labour markets differ by country, so findings from one country do not transfer automatically.

en.title: Education Budgeting and Resource Management
en.short: Budget types, preparation, records, procurement, control and how budgets link to plans.

sections.heading: Budgets and plans
sections.text: A budget is a plan in money for a set period. A recurrent budget covers running costs such as salaries, books and utilities. A capital budget covers long-lasting items such as buildings and equipment. Line-item budgets list spending by object; programme budgets group spending by activity or goal. Budgets serve planning, coordination, authorisation and control. They connect to plans because a school development plan or education sector plan states priorities, and the budget shows what can be afforded. Without that link, spending follows habit rather than need.

sections.heading: Preparing and monitoring
sections.text: Preparation follows a cycle: estimate needs, cost them, draft, approve, implement, monitor and review. Monitoring compares actual spending with the approved budget. Variance is the difference between the two. School records make this possible: cash book, vote book, receipts, ledger, inventory and store records. For example, a school plans 1,000,000 units: 550,000 for instruction, 250,000 for repairs and 200,000 for administration. Actual spending is 500,000, 250,000 and 230,000, total 980,000. Instruction is 50,000 under budget; administration is 30,000 over. The manager asks why and corrects next term.

sections.heading: Procurement and stores
sections.text: Procurement is buying goods and services. Good practice separates request, approval, purchase, receipt and payment. It uses needs assessment, quotations or tenders, purchase orders, delivery notes and invoices. Stores records show stock in, stock out and balances; regular checks reduce loss. Controls include segregation of duties, so one person does not order, receive and pay alone; written authorisation; competitive buying; and safe storage. These controls protect scarce funds and help books and equipment reach classrooms.

sections.heading: Accountability and learning
sections.text: Accountability means being answerable for money and property. Internal control, internal audit and external audit check that rules are followed and records are true. Poor resource management causes leakages, stock-outs, unused funds, poor maintenance and low morale. When textbooks arrive late or repairs wait, teaching time is lost and learning suffers. Teachers support control by keeping class records, using materials carefully and reporting damage. The budget shapes learning, not just paperwork.

keyPoints: A budget is a plan in money, usually for one year, with recurrent and capital parts.
The budget cycle runs from preparation and approval to implementation, monitoring and review.
Variance = actual spending − budgeted amount; it shows where to investigate.
School records such as cash book, vote book, inventory and store records support monitoring.
Procurement controls include segregation of duties, written approval, competitive buying and safe storage.
Poor resource management causes leakages and stock-outs, which reduce teaching time and learning.

en.title: Comparative and International Education Economics
en.short: Comparing education systems, indicators, international assessments, policy borrowing and the role of context.

sections.heading: Comparing systems
sections.text: Comparative education economics studies how education systems differ in inputs, processes and outcomes. An education indicator is a number that summarises one part of a system, such as enrolment, completion, pupil-teacher ratio or spending per student. International assessments are tests given in many countries, for example PISA and TIMSS, but they cover particular ages and subjects and not every country takes part. Comparisons must use the same definition, year and age group; otherwise the numbers mislead.

sections.heading: Indicators and fairness
sections.text: A fair comparison checks what is counted. Pupil-teacher ratio = total enrolment ÷ number of teachers. If a school has 600 pupils and 20 teachers, the ratio is 600 ÷ 20 = 30:1. But if one country counts all teachers and another counts only qualified teachers, the ratios are not comparable. Spending should be compared in purchasing power parity (PPP), which adjusts for price differences, not raw currency. A higher score in an international assessment may reflect a richer sample, more test practice or a narrower curriculum, not simply better teaching.

sections.heading: Policy borrowing
sections.text: Policy borrowing, also called policy transfer, means adopting an idea or practice from another country. It often starts with international comparisons or league tables. A policy that works in one country may fail in another because context differs: teacher training, funding, school governance, language, inequality and implementation capacity. For example, suppose a Nigerian state ministry copies a high-stakes exit exam from a country with well-trained markers and reliable data, but its own schools lack books and its marking system is weak. The exam may narrow teaching or increase dropout instead of raising learning.

sections.heading: Comparing well
sections.text: Start with a clear question. Use comparable data, state the year and definition, and adjust money for PPP. Check coverage: who is missing from the data? Triangulate (cross-check) international evidence with local studies and pilot before scaling. Treat league tables (rankings) with caution and avoid assuming that one system is simply better. The aim is to learn, not to copy blindly.

keyPoints: Comparative education economics compares systems using indicators such as enrolment, completion, pupil-teacher ratio and spending per student.
A fair comparison uses the same definition, year and age group, and adjusts money for purchasing power parity (PPP).
Pupil-teacher ratio = total enrolment ÷ number of teachers; spending per student = total spending ÷ enrolment.
International assessments such as PISA and TIMSS give useful evidence but cover particular ages, subjects and countries.
Policy borrowing means adopting another country’s policy; it can fail when context differs in teacher training, funding, governance or implementation capacity.
Compare to learn, not to copy: check coverage, triangulate with local evidence and pilot before scaling.

en.title: Research Methods in Education Economics
en.short: Research questions, literature review, designs, sampling, instruments, ethics and basic analysis for small studies.

sections.heading: Questions and review
sections.text: A research question states exactly what a study will answer. In education economics it should be focused, answerable with available data, and linked to a decision, such as whether a feeding programme raises attendance. A literature review groups earlier studies by theme, compares methods and findings, and states the gap your question fills. Record sources for accurate citation.

sections.heading: Designs and sampling
sections.text: Quantitative designs measure numbers, for example surveys, quasi-experiments (comparisons without random assignment) or analysis of school records. Qualitative designs explore meaning through interviews, focus groups, case studies or documents. Mixed methods combine both. The population is everyone you want to study; the sample is the part you collect data from. Probability sampling, such as random or stratified sampling, supports generalisation. Non-probability sampling, such as purposive sampling, is common in qualitative work but limits generalisation. Sample size depends on the design and analysis, so check a methods text rather than a fixed number.

sections.heading: Instruments and ethics
sections.text: An instrument is the tool used to collect data: a questionnaire, interview guide, test or observation schedule. Pilot it with a small group and revise unclear items. Quantitative instruments need validity, meaning they measure the intended construct, and reliability, meaning consistent results. Qualitative studies aim for trustworthiness through careful recording and checking. Ethics require informed consent, voluntary participation, confidentiality and no harm. Research with children usually needs guardian consent and child assent (the child’s own agreement), plus ethics approval and school permission. Protect data and report honestly.

sections.heading: Analysis and proposal
sections.text: Quantitative analysis uses percentages, means and cross-tabulations. The mean is the sum of scores divided by the number of scores: mean = Σx ÷ n. A percentage is part ÷ whole × 100. If 18 of 24 teachers return a questionnaire, the response rate is 18 ÷ 24 × 100 = 75%. Use inferential tests when the design and sample support them. Qualitative analysis often uses thematic analysis: code the text, group codes into themes, and support each theme with evidence. A small proposal states the question, review, design, sample, instruments, ethics and analysis.

keyPoints: A research question must be focused, answerable and linked to a real education decision.
A literature review compares studies and identifies the gap, not just summarises them.
Quantitative designs use numbers; qualitative designs explore meaning; mixed methods combine both.
Probability sampling supports generalisation, while purposive sampling is common in qualitative work but limits it.
Ethics require informed consent, confidentiality, no harm, and guardian consent plus child assent for research with children.
The mean is Σx ÷ n and a percentage is (part ÷ whole) × 100; use inferential tests only when the design supports them.

en.title: Professional Ethics for Economics Teachers
en.short: Teacher professionalism, fairness, confidentiality, assessment integrity, diversity and conflicts of interest.
