sections.heading: Professionalism and codes
sections.text: Professional ethics are the standards a teacher is expected to follow. Teacher professionalism includes preparation, punctuality, respect, honesty and continuing learning. Many countries have a code of conduct. The Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN) publishes one; other countries use teaching councils, ministries or unions. No single code applies everywhere. Read your own code and school policy, and follow the law. A code gives principles, not ready answers.

sections.heading: Fairness and confidentiality
sections.text: Fairness means treating students consistently, without favouritism or discrimination. Economics examples should not mock poor households or regions. Confidentiality covers grades, family circumstances, health and behaviour records. Share information only with those who need it. In economics, data from class surveys must be anonymised. A teacher who discusses a student’s low score in the staffroom without need breaches confidentiality.

sections.heading: Assessment integrity
sections.text: Assessment integrity means marks reflect learning. Use clear criteria, mark all scripts to the same standard, and keep records. Do not coach students on live test questions, change marks without evidence, or let personal liking affect grades. In quantitative work, check calculations and apply the same method to every script. If a student is accused of cheating, follow the school procedure, hear the student, and avoid public humiliation.

sections.heading: Diversity and conflicts
sections.text: Diversity includes language, religion, ethnicity, gender, disability and income. Use inclusive examples and avoid stereotypes. Conflicts of interest arise when a teacher’s private interest could affect duty, such as paid tutoring of one’s own students, selling textbooks or materials to them, or accepting gifts. Disclose the conflict and follow policy. Case: Mrs Bello teaches economics and runs private lessons. A weak student asks to pay for extra coaching before an examination. She should check school rules, avoid giving unfair advantage, and refer the request to the head. If private tutoring is allowed, she must not use it to reveal examination content.

keyPoints: Professional ethics are standards of conduct supported by codes and school policy, and they differ by country.
Fairness requires consistent treatment and marking, with no favouritism or discrimination.
Confidentiality protects student records and personal information; share only on a need-to-know basis.
Assessment integrity means marks and grades reflect learning, with clear criteria and checked calculations.
Diversity calls for inclusive examples and respect for language, religion, ethnicity, gender, disability and income.
Disclose conflicts of interest, such as tutoring your own students, and follow local rules.

en.title: Advanced Economics of Education
en.short: Human capital, signalling, production, intergenerational transmission and market failure in education.

sections.heading: Human capital models
sections.text: Human capital theory treats schooling as investment in skills that raise productivity and earnings. It compares costs with discounted benefits. The rule is net present value: PV = Σ (B(t) − C(t)) ÷ (1 + r)^t, where r is the discount rate and t is the year. If PV is positive, the investment pays. Example: extra earnings of 20,000 for three years at 10% discount are 18,181.82 + 16,528.93 + 15,026.30 = 49,737.05. Against a cost of 40,000, net PV is 9,737.05. It assumes people can borrow at the market rate and that returns are known.

sections.heading: Signalling and screening
sections.text: Signalling models, associated with Spence, say education may mainly reveal pre-existing ability. A worker who finds study easier gains a credential at lower cost, so the credential signals ability to employers. Screening is the employer’s use of that signal. Human capital says schooling creates skills; signalling says it sorts people. Evidence from returns to degrees suggests sorting is real but rarely the whole story. Expanding credentials may lower their informational value.

sections.heading: Production and transmission
sections.text: Education production functions relate outcomes, such as test scores, to inputs: teachers, class size, materials, peers and family background. Value added measures a school’s contribution after allowing for prior attainment. Estimates vary, and input effects are often small and context-dependent. Intergenerational transmission means parental education, income and health shape children’s outcomes through resources, expectations, genes and neighbourhoods. It helps explain persistent advantage. A family with educated parents can buy books and tutoring, so the child starts ahead; schools may widen or narrow that gap.

sections.heading: Market failure and equity
sections.text: Market failure occurs when private choices do not produce an efficient outcome. Credit constraints stop poor students borrowing against future earnings; information is uneven because families cannot easily judge school quality; and schooling creates externalities, benefits to others such as lower crime or better public health. These justify public funding and regulation, but not every subsidy is efficient. Equity concerns fair access and outcomes; efficiency concerns more learning per resource. The two can conflict, for example in targeting high-cost students. Policy should compare models and evidence openly.

keyPoints: Human capital theory compares discounted future benefits with current costs; net present value is PV = Σ (B(t) − C(t)) ÷ (1 + r)^t.
Signalling and screening models treat education as a signal of ability, not only as a producer of skills.
Education production functions relate outcomes to inputs, and value added adjusts for prior attainment.
Intergenerational transmission links parental resources and education to children’s outcomes.
Market failure in education arises from credit constraints, uneven information and externalities.
Equity and efficiency can conflict, so policy should compare models and evidence openly.

en.title: Econometric Evaluation of Education Policies
en.short: Causal inference, RCTs, natural experiments, DiD, IV and RD for education policy.

sections.heading: Causal questions
sections.text:
Evaluation asks what difference a policy made against what would have happened without it. The counterfactual is that unseen alternative. Because schools, students and regions differ, simple before-and-after or treated-versus-untreated comparisons can confuse selection with effect. Causal inference tries to isolate the policy effect.

A randomised controlled trial (RCT) assigns schools, teachers or students by chance to treatment or control. With good randomisation and low attrition, groups are comparable in expectation, so an outcome difference estimates the effect. RCTs are transparent and credible, but costly, ethically difficult, and limited in scale or context. Compliance and spillovers need care.

sections.heading: DiD and IV
sections.text:
Difference-in-differences (DiD) compares changes over time. Effect = (treated after − treated before) − (control after − control before). Its key assumption is parallel trends: without the policy, groups would have followed similar paths. Example: treated scores rise from 50 to 60 (+10); control scores rise from 48 to 54 (+6); DiD = 10 − 6 = 4 points. DiD is simple and uses routine data, but trends may differ.

Instrumental variables (IV) use a variable that shifts treatment but affects outcomes only through treatment. It must be relevant and satisfy exclusion. Natural experiments use rules not chosen by individuals; IV can exploit them, but weak or invalid instruments bias results; it estimates a local average effect for those moved by the instrument.

sections.heading: RD and policy
sections.text:
Regression discontinuity (RD) exploits a cutoff. If a scholarship needs an exam score of 60, students above and below are similar except for eligibility. Comparing them estimates the effect at the cutoff, provided scores cannot be manipulated and outcomes change smoothly otherwise. RD is credible but local, so it may not generalise far from the threshold.

For policy, report effect size with confidence intervals, not just significance. Ask for whom, at what cost, and whether delivery can be replicated. A four-point gain may matter if cheap and scalable, but not if it fades or excludes weaker students.

keyPoints: Causal evaluation compares policy outcomes with a credible counterfactual, not simple before-and-after differences.
RCTs estimate effects when randomisation is sound and attrition low; they face cost, ethics and context limits.
DiD effect = (treated after − treated before) − (control after − control before), assuming parallel trends.
IV requires relevance and exclusion; it identifies a local effect for people moved by the instrument.
RD compares units just above and below a cutoff and estimates a local effect at that threshold.
Policy interpretation needs effect size, confidence intervals, cost, scale and equity, not significance alone.

en.title: Advanced Education Finance and Governance
en.short: Financing mixes, vouchers, public-private partnerships, decentralisation, accountability and regulation.

sections.heading: Financing arrangements
sections.text: Education finance asks who pays, when and through which channel. Sources include public budgets, household fees, donors, employers and community contributions. Public funding can equalise access and spread costs, but may be inefficient or captured by elites. Fees can raise revenue and signal quality, but they can exclude poor students. Most systems use a mix, and the balance varies by country and level of education. A financing arrangement is not neutral: it shapes who enrols, what schools offer and how results are measured.

sections.heading: Vouchers and partnerships
sections.text: A voucher is a government-funded entitlement that a family can spend at an approved school. Advocates say it gives choice, pressure on weak schools and access for poor families. Critics say it can segregate students, leave the hardest-to-serve behind and drain funds from public schools; results depend on voucher design, school capacity and transport. A public-private partnership (PPP) is a long-term contract in which a private firm builds, operates or supplies a public education service. It can bring capital and management skill, but can create hidden costs, weak contract monitoring and reduced public control. In an invented case, a district contracts a firm to build and maintain ten schools while the public authority sets fees and learning standards; the contract must specify performance, penalties and public access. Outcomes vary widely by country.

sections.heading: Decentralisation and accountability
sections.text: Decentralisation transfers decisions to districts, municipalities or schools. Supporters argue it improves local fit, speed and participation. Opponents warn of unequal capacity, control by local elites and duties without funds. Accountability means that officials and schools must answer for spending and results. It works better when information on budgets and learning is public, and when parents and auditors can act. Regulation sets entry, fees, curriculum, safety and quality rules. Good regulation protects students; excessive or poorly enforced rules can stifle providers or be ignored.

keyPoints: Financing arrangements decide who pays and therefore who gains access.
Vouchers can expand choice but may worsen segregation unless designed and funded carefully.
PPPs can add capital and skills but need strong contracts, monitoring and public accountability.
Decentralisation can improve local fit but may widen inequality where local capacity is weak.
Accountability requires public information and real consequences for results.
Regulation must protect quality without blocking good providers, and its effects vary by country.

en.title: Research Seminar and Dissertation
en.short: From proposal to defence: literature review, design, ethics, data analysis and academic writing.

sections.heading: Proposal and literature
sections.text:
A research proposal is a short plan stating the problem, question, aims and method. Present it in the seminar for criticism before collecting data.

The literature review maps what is known, identifies gaps and shows how your question follows. Use recent, peer-reviewed sources and official statistics, and record every source for accurate citation. The standard is traceability: another researcher should follow your argument from question to evidence.

sections.heading: Design and ethics
sections.text:
Choose a design that answers your question. Quantitative designs test relationships with numbers; qualitative designs explore meanings; mixed methods combine both. Define your population, sample and instruments, and pilot them.

Ethical approval, formal permission from a review committee, comes before data collection. Submit your protocol, obtain informed consent, protect confidentiality and store data securely. Rules differ by country and institution, so check requirements. In an invented case, Amina in Kano plans a mixed-methods study of school feeding and attendance: a survey of 300 students and interviews with 10 teachers. Her committee asks for parental consent for minors and a data storage plan.

sections.heading: Data and analysis
sections.text:
Collect data with an audit trail: dates, instrument versions, response rates and reasons for missing data. Analyse according to the design.

For surveys, report descriptive statistics and check reliability; for interviews, use thematic analysis and keep coding records. Standards of evidence include validity (measuring what you claim), reliability (consistency), triangulation (more than one source) and reflexivity (examining your influence). If Amina receives 240 replies from 300 students, her response rate is 240 ÷ 300 = 80%. She should report this and discuss non-response.

sections.heading: Writing and defence
sections.text:
Write in a plain academic style: one idea per paragraph, signposting, and claims supported by evidence. The dissertation includes introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion and conclusion.

In the oral defence, or viva, you explain and justify your choices and answer questions. Prepare a summary, anticipate weaknesses, and be honest about limitations. Examiners judge whether the work is coherent, ethical and defensible, not whether every result is significant.

keyPoints: A proposal states the question, aims and method, and is tested in the seminar before data collection.
The literature review must map existing knowledge and justify the gap, not just summarise sources.
Ethical approval is required before data collection; consent, confidentiality and secure storage are core.
Choose a design that fits the question, and pilot instruments before full data collection.
Report validity, reliability, triangulation and limitations; for surveys, response rate = replies ÷ invited × 100.
In the viva, justify your choices honestly and acknowledge limitations.
